charts.title: Country of origin
charts.question: What is your country of origin?
charts.takeaway: Two countries, the United States and Brazil, give almost half of the answers (47%).

charts.title: Where they live now
charts.question: Where are you currently living?

charts.title: Age
charts.question: What is your age?
charts.takeaway: This is a young group: about two in three respondents are between 23 and 37.

charts.title: Gender identity
charts.question: What is your gender identity?

charts.title: Underrepresented communities
charts.question: Do you belong to any of these underrepresented communities?
charts.takeaway: Belonging to an underrepresented group is common here: besides Women in Tech (54%), about one in five is neurodivergent and one in five is LGBTQ+.

charts.title: Age and gender together
charts.question: Number of people in each age band (Q4), women and men side by side (Q5).
charts.takeaway: Women are the majority in every age group, with the highest share among people aged 23–32 (74%).

charts.title: Where people moved
charts.question: Where people come from (Q2) and where they live now (Q3).
charts.takeaway: One in five lives outside the country they come from, and one in seven changed region. Europe → North America and Latin America → Europe are the most common routes.

charts.title: Years in conversation design
charts.question: How long have you been working in the conversation design space?
charts.takeaway: Experience is short: 8 in 10 have six years or less in conversation design.

charts.title: Level at the current job
charts.question: What is your level at your current job?
charts.takeaway: Only 11% are entry-level, while 70% are mid-level or senior.

charts.title: Where they worked in the past 12 months
charts.question: During the past 12 months, where did you work as a Conversation Design Practitioner or perform functions directly related to Conversation Design?
charts.takeaway: Product companies lead in the three largest regions, but in Europe agencies and consultancies weigh far more: 42%, against 21% overall.

charts.title: Remote work
charts.question: Do you currently work remotely?
charts.takeaway: Working fully on site is rare (2%). Europe is the hybrid exception: 58% hybrid.

charts.title: Type of workplace
charts.question: What type of workplace do you currently work at?
charts.takeaway: The role has no single home: in-house teams and product teams are level, at about 35% each.

charts.title: Scope of the work
charts.question: What is the scope of your current work?
charts.takeaway: Reach changes with region: most in North America work on global products (58%), most in Latin America on local ones (60%).

charts.title: Company size (employees)
charts.question: What is the size of your company?
charts.takeaway: The field is split by company size: 37% work alone or in organisations of up to 200 people, and 34% in ones with more than 5,000.

charts.title: Size of the conversation design team
charts.question: How many people are in your organization’s Conversation Design team, including full-time and contract roles?
charts.takeaway: Many design alone or nearly alone: 4 in 10 are the only designer or in a team of 2–3.

charts.title: Annual salary (USD)
charts.question: What is your annual salary range (in USD)? Full-time equivalent if part-time. (optional; shown in merged bands)

charts.title: Career statements
charts.question: Rate the following career-related statements based on your experience.
charts.takeaway: People feel more challenged by the work (66% agree) than valued for it (53%).

charts.title: What would sustain a rating of 5
charts.question: What actions or changes could help achieve or sustain a rating of 5? If possible, please share what influenced your rating.
charts.takeaway: When people explain their career rating, generative AI comes up most (37%), then recognition of the role (33%). In Latin America, recognition leads (51%).

charts.title: Career trail: years in the field and level
charts.question: People per combination of years in the field (Q7) and current level (Q8).
charts.takeaway: The field promotes early: many people with 4–6 years are already senior.

charts.title: How people work, by region
charts.question: Work arrangement (Q10) in each region where people live (Q3).
charts.takeaway: Fully remote dominates in the Americas; Europe is the hybrid region.

charts.title: Feeling valued, by team size
charts.question: Average agreement with “My work is valued within my organisation” (Q16) by size of the conversation design team (Q14), with an 80% interval.
charts.takeaway: Teams of 2 to 5 feel least valued. Teams of more than 50 feel it most, but the rise is not steady.

charts.title: Salary bands at their real width
charts.question: Annual salary range (Q15), drawn with each band at its true width in dollars.
charts.takeaway: 51% of salary answers are under $50k, where the bands are narrow and the bars are tallest.

charts.title: Job titles, grouped
charts.question: What is your current job title? (titles grouped into families)
charts.takeaway: More than half have another job title: only 47% are in the Conversation Designer group.

charts.title: Daily work, in their words
charts.question: Briefly describe your daily work as a Conversation Designer, as if explaining it to a stakeholder in your organization or context.
charts.takeaway: Flows are the core of the job. Around them, stakeholders, analysis and building with developers each appear for about a third.

charts.title: How they deliver value
charts.question: What are the primary ways you deliver value as a Conversation Design practitioner in your organization or context?
charts.takeaway: People tie their value to user experience and business goals much more than to revenue: only 23% name conversion or revenue.

charts.title: Activities that take most time
charts.question: Which of these activities do you spend most time on?
charts.takeaway: Craft is still the daily core: conversation UX and scripts are each picked by more than half. Prompt engineering is at 23%.

charts.title: Modality worked with the most
charts.question: Which modality have you worked with the most?
charts.takeaway: Chat is nearly everywhere, but voice is a large part of the work in North America (58%) and Europe (52%).

charts.title: How often they collaborate
charts.question: How often do you collaborate with teams within your organization or with external stakeholders?

charts.title: Education and training
charts.question: What is your formal education or structured training related to your work in Conversation Design?
charts.takeaway: There is no single way in: work experience, degrees and courses each count for half or more, and 28% came self-taught from another background.

charts.title: Fields of study and training
charts.question: If you have a formal degree or structured training, please specify the degree, certifications, or related field.
charts.takeaway: Language is a big root of the field: linguistics and languages (43%) come close to courses and bootcamps (45%).

charts.title: How they define the discipline
charts.question: How do you define or explain the discipline of conversation design?
charts.takeaway: People don’t share one definition of the discipline: no single idea appears in more than 37% of answers.

charts.title: Why it matters
charts.question: Why do you believe conversation design is important for businesses and users?
charts.takeaway: The value people describe is mostly user experience (46%) and savings (35%), far more than revenue (12%).

charts.title: What conversation design is not
charts.question: In your opinion, what ISN’T conversation design? What’s something most people get wrong?
charts.takeaway: The misunderstanding they most want to correct: conversation design is not just copywriting (54%).

charts.title: Specializations
charts.question: Which areas of conversation design do you specialize in?
charts.takeaway: Generative AI is already a skill for almost half (47%). Agentic AI (17%) and AI orchestration (9%) are still rare.

charts.title: What helped them learn the most
charts.question: Which resources have been the most effective in supporting your professional development?
charts.takeaway: People learn at work and from each other: 88% on the job, 58% with colleagues and mentors, 17% in company training.

charts.title: Local communities, people and content
charts.question: What local communities, professionals, or content (books, blogs, events) have helped you learn about conversation design? Please share your local recommendations.
charts.takeaway: Communities are the most recommended way to learn, ahead of courses and books. In North America, books come first.

charts.title: Most named resources
charts.question: What local communities, professionals, or content (books, blogs, events) have helped you learn about conversation design? Please share your local recommendations. (most named by respondents)
charts.takeaway: No resource is universal, and the favourites change by region: in Latin America, Bots Brasil is the most named (42% of only 26 answers).

charts.title: Specialisations that go together
charts.question: Of the people who chose each specialisation (Q26), the share who also chose each other one.
charts.takeaway: Specialisations come in bundles: people combine three or four, and some pairs appear together far more often than chance.

charts.title: Types of tools
charts.question: Which types of tools do you primarily use in your workflow?
charts.takeaway: The common kit is not technical: diagrams, spreadsheets and the conversation platform. Coding tools reach 10%.

charts.title: Why these tools matter
charts.question: Please share why these tools are important in your workflow or how you use them to support your work.
charts.takeaway: Half of those who explain their tools name making flows visible to others as a use.

charts.title: Named tools
charts.question: Please share why these tools are important in your workflow or how you use them to support your work. (tools named by respondents)
charts.takeaway: When people name a product, general-purpose tools come first; Voiceflow is the conversation platform named most (22%).

charts.title: Biggest challenges
charts.question: What is the biggest challenge you face in the practice of conversation design?
charts.takeaway: The top challenge is keeping quality despite project constraints (46%), ahead of the limits of AI itself (35%).

charts.title: Channels and platforms
charts.question: Which specific channels or platforms do you primarily develop solutions for?
charts.takeaway: There is no single main channel: voice leads in North America (58%) and WhatsApp in Latin America (61%).

charts.title: Challenges and the help they call for
charts.question: Biggest challenge (Q32) linked to the most important improvement needed (Q43) when the people who name the challenge choose that improvement clearly more often.
charts.takeaway: Each challenge points to its own remedy. The strongest link: 59% of those who chose “Communicating value to stakeholders” ask for “Greater stakeholder support”, against 45% of everyone (56 of 95 people).

charts.title: Which archetype uses which tools
charts.question: Share of each archetype using each type of tool (Q30).
charts.takeaway: Flow diagramming is common ground for most archetypes, but not for Strategists; data analysis, NLP training and coding split the archetypes most.

charts.title: Common ground or profile marker? Tools in two axes
charts.question: Each tool (Q30) placed by how many people use it and by the gap between the archetype that uses it most and least.
charts.takeaway: No tool is common ground: the three most used (flow diagramming, spreadsheets, the conversation platform) each split the archetypes by 56 points or more.

charts.title: Biggest challenge of 2024
charts.question: What do you believe was the biggest challenge faced by conversation designers in 2024?
charts.takeaway: Adopting generative AI was the shared challenge of the year, named three times as often as the next one.

charts.title: Most excited and most concerned
charts.question: Reflecting on 2024, what trends or shifts in the field of conversation design made you feel the most excited and the most concerned?
charts.takeaway: Asked what excited or worried them in 2024, three in four spoke about generative AI and language models.

charts.title: How 2024 went
charts.question: Rate the following statements based on your experience over the past year.
charts.takeaway: Tools improved more than understanding: 60% say tools got much better; 40% say businesses now understand the value better.

charts.title: What generative and agentic AI did to the field
charts.question: How do you think the rise of Agentic AI and Generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT, LLM-based assistants) has impacted the conversation design field?
charts.takeaway: AI did not do one thing to the role: new focus (32%), less demand (27%), new risks (23%) and a bigger role (19%).

charts.title: Essential for 2025
charts.question: Complete the sentence: One or two things that will be essential for every Conversation Design professional in 2025 are ___.
charts.takeaway: AI literacy is the skill people most expect to be essential, well ahead of technical skills.

charts.title: 2025 will be MORE about
charts.question: Complete the sentence: Conversation Design in 2025 will be MORE about ___
charts.takeaway: Expectations centre on design driven by generative AI (45%), with less agreement in Europe (30%).

charts.title: 2025 will be LESS about
charts.question: Complete the sentence: Conversation Design in 2025 will be LESS about ___
charts.takeaway: What people expect to fade is rigid and manual work: fixed flows and writing every line by hand.

charts.title: Most important improvement needed
charts.question: Looking forward, what is the most important improvement needed for Conversation Designers to succeed in the near future?
charts.takeaway: What would help most depends on place: training in Latin America (70%), stakeholder support in Europe (63%).

charts.title: Maturity of the field in 2025
charts.question: How do you perceive the current maturity of Conversation Design in 2025?
charts.takeaway: Only 5% see an established field; about 8 in 10 call it fragmented or still without standards.

charts.title: Expectations for 2025
charts.question: Rate the following statements based on your expectations for 2025.
charts.takeaway: People expect change more than growth: 77% see AI changing the work a lot, 53% expect more demand for designers.

charts.title: How the view of AI shapes the skills people call essential
charts.question: What AI did to the field (Q39) linked to themes people call essential for 2025 (Q40, open text grouped into themes).
charts.takeaway: How people read AI shapes the skills they call essential. The strongest link: 21% of those who chose “New ethics, hallucination and trust challenges” name “Ethics & responsible AI”, against 9% of everyone (13 of 61 people).

charts.title: 2024 in review against 2025 expectations
charts.question: Agreement with statements about 2024 (Q38) and expectations for 2025 (Q45), on the same five-point scale.
charts.takeaway: Almost everyone expects AI to change the field, but only about half expect more demand for designers.

charts.title: How people read AI predicts how they see demand
charts.question: Agreement that demand for conversational designers will grow (Q45), by what the person thinks AI did to the field (Q39).
charts.takeaway: Those who saw AI expand the role average 4.00 on demand growth; those who saw it reduce demand average 2.95.

charts.title: Length of the survey
charts.question: How did you feel about the length of this survey?
charts.takeaway: Two in three found the survey long.

charts.title: The survey and its future
charts.question: How do you perceive this survey and its continuity in the future?
charts.takeaway: Respondents want the answers back: 89% are interested in the results.

charts.title: Feedback and suggestions
charts.question: Feedback, suggestions, or any other helpful comments to improve the survey? Please share here.
charts.takeaway: Among the comments, praise comes first; the other requests spread across results, clarity, content, length and answer format.

charts.title: Responses over time
charts.question: Responses per week during the field period (27 January to 7 April 2025).
charts.takeaway: Half the answers (144 of 286) arrived in the first four weeks, and a second wave in the last two weeks brought 91 (32%).

charts.title: How long it took to answer
charts.question: Time from opening the form to sending it, for the responses where the form recorded it.
charts.takeaway: The typical respondent took 25 minutes; 48% finished in under 25.

charts.title: The survey journey
charts.question: Responses per week and the running total over the eleven weeks of field work, with the typical time to answer.
charts.takeaway: Answers came in two waves: half arrived in the first four weeks (144 of 286), and the last two weeks brought another 32%.

charts.title: From responses to charts
charts.question: How many responses each kind of chart rests on, and where groups are hidden.
charts.takeaway: Every chart starts from 286 responses; salary charts rest on 265, and on 232 when split by region.

charts.title: Gender by level
charts.question: What is your gender identity (Q5), by level at the current job (Q8)?

charts.title: How much does someone like me earn?
charts.question: Median annual salary (Q15) for each level (Q8) inside each region where people live (Q3).
charts.takeaway: At the same level, pay depends on where people live: a senior's median is $175k in North America and $23k in Latin America, about 7.8×.

charts.title: The gender pay gap is mostly a region gap
charts.question: Median annual salary (Q15) of women and men (Q5), overall and inside each region (Q3).
charts.takeaway: Overall, women's median is $43k against $65k for men. Inside North America it is $135k against $140k: the gap mostly disappears within a region.

charts.title: Every salary answer, by region
charts.question: Annual salary (Q15) of each respondent, one dot per person, in each region where people live (Q3).
charts.takeaway: The regions barely overlap: in Latin America 73% earn $25k or less, while the North American median is $135k.

charts.title: Pay by level, inside each place
charts.question: Median annual salary (Q15) at each job level (Q8), inside each region and country where people live (Q3).
charts.takeaway: Level matters, but place matters more: the median for a mid-level person in the United States is $115k; for a senior in Brazil it is $18k.

charts.title: Archetype pay inside each region
charts.question: Median annual salary (Q15) of each archetype inside each region where people live (Q3).
charts.takeaway: Agent Builders have the highest overall median, but inside North America Bridge Builders earn as much, and in Latin America every group sits between $13k and $23k: pay mostly follows where people live.

charts.title: Archetypes by region, level, gender and pay
charts.question: For each archetype: share living in North America and Latin America (Q3), share senior or above (Q8), share of women (Q5) and median pay (Q15).
charts.takeaway: The archetypes differ sharply in region, seniority and gender, not only in what they do.

charts.title: Pay by country, with a drill-down by region
Archetypes around the world: most common archetype in each region
charts.takeaway: The most common archetype changes with the region: Script Writer in North America (19%), Flow Craftsperson in Latin America (26%) and Bridge Builder in Europe (21%).

findings.title: Women in every group
findings.detail: 68% are women. They are the majority in every age band and every region: 72% in Latin America, 67% in North America, 64% in Europe.
findings.stat: 68% of respondents are women
findings.why: Not a quirk of one country: the profession itself is mostly women, unlike most tech roles.

findings.title: Three regions, almost equal
findings.detail: North America and Latin America hold 31% each, Europe 23%. All other regions together hold 14%, which reflects who the survey reached.
findings.stat: 86% live in North America, Latin America or Europe
findings.why: The survey speaks for the Americas and Europe. Asia, Africa and the Middle East are too small here to draw conclusions about.

findings.title: Brazil is the field's second home
findings.detail: By origin, Brazil (22%) is almost level with the United States (24%), well ahead of any other country.
findings.stat: 22% were born in Brazil, close to the US (24%)
findings.why: Brazil's community is as large as the US one, so results lean on two very different pay markets.

findings.title: Late twenties and thirties
findings.detail: Half are 28 to 37 years old (52%); 28–32 is the largest band at 29%.
findings.stat: 52% are 28 to 37 years old
findings.why: A field built mostly by one generation, which entered as chatbots became mainstream.

findings.title: One in five lives abroad
findings.detail: 20% live outside the country they come from and 14% changed region, mostly towards North America and Europe, where pay is higher.
findings.stat: 20% live outside their country of origin
findings.why: Conversation design travels: people move, mostly to where pay is higher.

findings.title: Identity beyond gender
findings.detail: Asked about underrepresented communities, 54% name women in tech and 19% LGBTQ+.
findings.stat: 54% identify with women in tech
findings.why: Representation goes beyond gender: one in five belongs to the LGBTQ+ community.

findings.title: A young field
findings.detail: 40% have three years or less in conversation design, and only 20% have seven or more.
findings.stat: 40% have 3 years or less in the field
findings.why: Most people learned the work in the chatbot and LLM era; few carry experience from earlier waves.

findings.title: Promoted early
findings.detail: 62% of people with 4–6 years in the field are already senior or above. Overall, half the respondents (51%) are senior or more.
findings.stat: 62% with 4–6 years are already senior or above
findings.why: Titles move fast in a young field: senior often means four or five years of experience.

findings.title: Small or solo teams
findings.detail: 42% work alone or in a team of two or three conversation designers.
findings.stat: 42% work alone or with 1–2 other designers
findings.why: Many designers have no peer to review their work, which shapes how they learn and how they are valued.

findings.title: Small teams feel less valued
findings.detail: 53% of solo designers feel valued at work, against 67% in teams of 21 or more.
findings.stat: 53% vs 67% feel valued: solo vs teams of 21+
findings.why: Having peers who understand the work seems to help it be recognised.

findings.title: Remote by default
findings.detail: 60% are fully remote and only 2% work from an office. Europe is the exception, with 58% hybrid.
findings.stat: 60% work fully remote
findings.why: Hiring is already global, which puts people from different pay markets in the same teams.

findings.title: One field, two pay markets
findings.detail: The middle half earns between $18k and $115k a year: a gap that mostly separates regions, not levels.
findings.stat: $18k–$115k a year: where the middle half of salaries sits
findings.why: An average salary would describe nobody: read pay by region.

findings.title: Impact before recognition
findings.detail: 66% feel challenged to make a meaningful impact, but only 53% feel their work is valued. What would make it a 5: AI's effect on the role (37%), then recognition (33%).
findings.stat: 66% vs 53% feel challenged vs feel valued
findings.why: People feel their work matters more than their organisation shows it does.

findings.title: Place before level
findings.detail: A senior's median is $175k in North America and $23k in Latin America, 7.8 times more.
findings.stat: 7.8× a senior earns in North America vs Latin America
findings.why: For pay, where you live counts far more than how senior you are.

findings.title: The gender gap is mostly a region gap
findings.detail: Women's median is $43k against $65k for men overall, but $135k against $140k inside North America.
findings.stat: $135k · $140k women · men inside North America
findings.why: Women are a larger share in Latin America, where pay is lowest; compared inside one region, the gap almost closes.

findings.title: Women thin out at the top
findings.detail: Women are 75% of mid-level roles and 38% of director, VP and C-level roles.
findings.stat: 75% → 38% women at mid-level → at director and above
findings.why: The majority at the base does not reach leadership in the same proportion.

findings.title: Valued grows with level and team
findings.detail: Feeling valued rises from 3.13 at entry level to 3.66 at principal, and to 3.73 in teams of 21 or more (scale 1 to 5).
findings.stat: 3.13 → 3.66 feeling valued, entry → principal (1–5)
findings.why: Recognition comes with seniority and with having a team around you.

findings.title: Solo in smaller companies
findings.detail: 35% of people in companies of up to 200 employees are the only conversation designer, against 7% in companies of 5,000 or more.
findings.stat: 35% vs 7% are the only designer: small vs large companies
findings.why: In smaller companies the role is usually a team of one.

findings.title: Valued and growth go together
findings.detail: Among those who feel valued (4 or 5), 70% also see clear career growth; among those who do not (1 or 2), only 30% do.
findings.stat: 70% vs 30% see growth: valued vs not valued
findings.why: Recognition and career prospects rise and fall together.

findings.title: Moving pays, in Europe
findings.detail: In Europe, people who came from another country earn a median of $65k against $48k for those who did not move (25 and 42 people). In North America the newcomers earn less: $115k against $135k.
findings.stat: $65k vs $48k in Europe: came from abroad vs did not move
findings.why: A signal, not a rule: the groups are small, but moving does not pay off the same way everywhere.

findings.title: One in four works for clients
findings.detail: 27% worked in an agency or as freelancers in the past year.
findings.stat: 27% worked in an agency or freelance
findings.why: A large share builds for several companies, not inside one product.

findings.title: Most work across borders
findings.detail: 42% work globally, across countries or regions.
findings.stat: 42% work across countries or regions
findings.why: Many designers write for audiences and languages beyond their own.

findings.title: A title takes hold
findings.detail: Almost half (47%) hold the title Conversation Designer; the next title, UX Writer or Content Designer, has 14%.
findings.stat: 47% hold the title Conversation Designer
findings.why: A shared name is a sign of a maturing profession.

findings.title: Voice is regional
findings.detail: Chat is near universal (81%). Voice is common in North America (58%) and Europe (52%) but rare in Latin America (16%).
findings.stat: 58% vs 16% work with voice: North vs Latin America
findings.why: What counts as conversation design depends on the market: voice in the north, chat in Latin America.

findings.title: Few work across channels
findings.detail: Only 28% work with both chat and voice; multimodal work (19%) is still a niche.
findings.stat: 28% work with both chat and voice
findings.why: Multichannel and multimodal skills are still rare, and could set people apart.

findings.title: Valued for experience, then for business
findings.detail: 69% deliver value by improving engagement and satisfaction, 59% by aligning flows to KPIs, 50% by lowering support costs.
findings.stat: 69% deliver value through engagement and satisfaction
findings.why: Designers argue in user terms first; business metrics come second.

findings.title: Close to product, far from leadership
findings.detail: 86% work often or daily with product and tech teams; only 33% with leadership.
findings.stat: 86% vs 33% work often with product and tech vs leadership
findings.why: The work is shaped by product teams, but rarely discussed where budgets are decided.

findings.title: Agent Builders earn the most
findings.detail: The Agent Builder median is $95k, against $23k for the Flow Craftsperson. Half of Agent Builders (52%) live in North America, against 20% of Craftspeople.
findings.stat: $95k vs $23k median: Agent Builder vs Flow Craftsperson
findings.why: Part of the gap is the work, part is where each archetype lives: compare inside each region.

findings.title: Optimizers are almost all women
findings.detail: 89% of Optimizers are women, against 55% of Agent Builders and Bridge Builders.
findings.stat: 89% of Optimizers are women
findings.why: The more technical archetypes are where men are best represented.

findings.title: Learned on the job
findings.detail: 88% say on-the-job learning helped them most. Formal post-secondary programs help only 13%.
findings.stat: 88% say learning on the job helped most
findings.why: There is no standard path in; schools have not caught up with the role.

findings.title: Degrees, but not in conversation design
findings.detail: 52% have a degree in a related field, and linguistics or languages is named by 43% of those who listed their studies.
findings.stat: 52% have a degree in a related field
findings.why: Linguistics and languages are a common way in, alongside design.

findings.title: Defined by what it is not
findings.detail: Asked what it is not, 54% say it is not just copywriting or scripting, and 32% not just chatbots.
findings.stat: 54% say it is not just copywriting or scripting
findings.why: Practitioners still spend energy explaining that the work is more than writing bot lines.

findings.title: GenAI is now a mainstream skill
findings.detail: 47% already specialise in generative AI; agentic AI (17%) and AI orchestration (9%) are the next frontier.
findings.stat: 47% already specialise in generative AI
findings.why: Generative AI moved from novelty to everyday skill within a year.

findings.title: Its value, in two languages
findings.detail: People justify the work by user experience (46%) and by cost savings (35%).
findings.stat: 46% · 35% justify it by user experience · by cost savings
findings.why: The case for the work is made in two currencies: experience and cost.

findings.title: Communities teach
findings.detail: Communities and groups are the most cited learning resource (41%), ahead of courses (34%).
findings.stat: 41% name communities as a learning resource
findings.why: Peer communities fill the gap left by formal education.

findings.title: Seniority moves the work to strategy
findings.detail: 60% at principal level and above specialise in strategy, against 9% at entry level.
findings.stat: 9% → 60% specialise in strategy, entry → principal+
findings.why: Growing in the role means moving from building flows to shaping strategy.

findings.title: Juniors ask for training
findings.detail: 59% at entry level ask for better training, against 36% at principal level and above.
findings.stat: 59% vs 36% ask for training: entry vs principal+
findings.why: The lack of formal paths weighs most on those just starting.

findings.title: Diagrams and spreadsheets
findings.detail: 77% use flow diagrams and 58% spreadsheets; Google Sheets is the most named tool (45%), ahead of Figma (30%).
findings.stat: 77% use flow diagrams
findings.why: Generic tools beat specialised ones: the craft lives in flows and tables.

findings.title: Little code
findings.detail: Only 10% use code editors and 24% NLP training tools.
findings.stat: 10% use code editors
findings.why: Most designers work above the code, which may change as agents spread.

findings.title: Constraints, more than AI
findings.detail: The top challenge is quality under project constraints (46%), ahead of AI and NLP limits (35%).
findings.stat: 46% struggle with quality under project constraints
findings.why: The hardest part is delivering quality with little time and budget, not the technology.

findings.title: Value is hard to show
findings.detail: 34% struggle to communicate their value and 29% to measure success.
findings.stat: 34% struggle to communicate their value
findings.why: Without shared metrics, designers struggle to prove impact.

findings.title: No shared toolkit
findings.detail: Every widely used tool splits the archetypes by 56 points or more.
findings.stat: 56+ pts gap between archetypes on every common tool
findings.why: Each type of designer works with a different kit; there is no single standard stack.

findings.title: Web and voice, level
findings.detail: Web chat and voice or IVR tie as the main channel, each at 34%.
findings.stat: 34% · 34% main channel: web chat · voice or IVR
findings.why: Both channels still matter, so skills in each stay relevant.

findings.title: The GenAI year
findings.detail: 63% name adopting GenAI and LLMs as their biggest challenge of 2024, and 75% name it as what excited or worried them most.
findings.stat: 63% say GenAI was the biggest challenge of 2024
findings.why: 2024 was defined by one topic, which left little room for anything else.

findings.title: Tools ran ahead of understanding
findings.detail: 60% say tools improved in 2024; only 40% say businesses understand the value of the work better.
findings.stat: 60% vs 40% better tools vs better business understanding
findings.why: Organisations adopted AI tools faster than they understood what designers bring.

findings.title: Opportunities lag
findings.detail: Only 40% saw better career opportunities in 2024.
findings.stat: 40% saw better career opportunities in 2024
findings.why: Better technology did not turn into better careers in the same year.

findings.title: Four readings of AI
findings.detail: A shift to prompting (32%), less demand for traditional skills (27%), new ethics risks (23%), a bigger role (19%): no consensus.
findings.stat: 32 · 27 · 23 · 19% four effects of AI, none a majority
findings.why: The field has not agreed on what AI did to it.

findings.title: Newcomers worry more about trust
findings.detail: 28% of those with up to 3 years say AI's main effect is new ethics and trust risks, against 18% of those with 7 or more.
findings.stat: 28% vs 18% see ethics risk first: ≤3 years vs 7+
findings.why: Those who arrived with LLMs worry more about trust and ethics than veterans.

findings.title: Certain change, uncertain demand
findings.detail: 77% expect AI to change the field significantly in 2025; 53% expect demand for designers to grow.
findings.stat: 77% vs 53% expect big change vs expect more demand
findings.why: Everyone agrees the work will change; far fewer are sure there will be more of it.

findings.title: Europe is the least sure
findings.detail: 43% in Europe expect demand to grow, against 56–57% in the Americas.
findings.stat: 43% in Europe expect demand to grow
findings.why: European designers are the most cautious about growth.

findings.title: AI literacy is the new baseline
findings.detail: 49% name AI and LLM literacy as essential for 2025, far ahead of any other skill.
findings.stat: 49% call AI and LLM literacy essential
findings.why: Understanding models is now part of the job, not a specialisation.

findings.title: Goodbye rigid flows
findings.detail: 33% expect less rule-based bots and 28% less manual scripting.
findings.stat: 33% expect fewer rule-based bots
findings.why: Scripted, rule-based design is expected to shrink.

findings.title: Not mature yet
findings.detail: 43% call the field fragmented and 38% evolving without standards; 5% call it established.
findings.stat: 5% call the field established
findings.why: Without standards, each company defines the role its own way.

findings.title: Training first
findings.detail: Better training is the improvement asked for most (50%), then stakeholder support (44%) and better pay (40%).
findings.stat: 50% ask for better training first
findings.why: People ask for training before pay: they want a path to grow.

findings.title: How you read AI predicts your outlook
findings.detail: Expected demand growth averages 4.00 among those who say AI expanded the role and 2.95 among those who say it reduced demand.
findings.stat: 4.00 vs 2.95 expected demand: AI expanded the role vs reduced demand
findings.why: Optimism about the field follows how people read AI's effect on it.

findings.title: Long, by feeling
findings.detail: 66% found the survey long, though the typical respondent took 25 minutes.
findings.stat: 66% found the survey long
findings.why: The next edition will be shorter.

findings.title: They want the results
findings.detail: 87% are interested in the results.
findings.stat: 87% want to see the results
findings.why: Interest in shared data is high, and this report answers it.

findings.title: Length does not deter
findings.detail: 48% of those who found it long would take part again, close to 53% of those who found it right.
findings.stat: 48% vs 53% would answer again: found it long vs right
findings.why: A long survey did not stop people from wanting to take part again.

findings.title: Two waves
findings.detail: Half the answers came in the first four weeks, a second wave in the last two.
findings.stat: 2 waves of answers: launch and final weeks
findings.why: Reminders worked: the final push brought a second wave of answers.

findings.title: Time given
findings.detail: Together, respondents gave about 119 hours to the survey.
findings.stat: 119 h given by respondents in total
findings.why: About 119 hours of volunteer time sit behind these numbers.

archetypes.name: The Flow Craftsperson
archetypes.tagline: Shapes the conversation itself: flows, scripts, interface.
archetypes.summary: Works on the conversation as an experience: the UX, the flow, the script.

archetypes.name: The Script Writer
archetypes.tagline: Writes the words, and increasingly the training data.
archetypes.summary: Starts from UX writing, scripts and flows, and has added generative AI and model training to the toolkit.

archetypes.name: The Bridge Builder
archetypes.summary: Combines strategy, service design and project and stakeholder management with solid conversation UX.

archetypes.name: The Model Trainer
archetypes.tagline: Trains and tunes the model behind the dialogue.
archetypes.summary: The strongest on AI and NLP training, generative AI and data analysis.

archetypes.name: The Optimizer
archetypes.tagline: Reads the data and tunes the conversation.
archetypes.summary: Spends the time on data, analysis and optimisation, and ties the work to conversion and measurable results.

archetypes.name: The Strategist
archetypes.tagline: Frames the problem and carries it to the organisation.
archetypes.summary: Works on strategy and roadmaps, research and testing, and service design, less on writing the dialogue itself.

archetypes.name: The Agent Builder
archetypes.tagline: Builds with models, prompts and agents.
archetypes.summary: Specialises in generative and agentic AI, writes prompts and orchestrates tools.
